PayGuard is now a container. The next question is **where it lives**. Every cloud offers the same basic menu at different levels of "how much do you want to manage yourself". The right choice depends mostly on **traffic shape, team size and budget**.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn
- The four ways to run a model in the cloud, from raw servers to fully managed ML
- The matching services on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure
- How always-on servers and pay-per-request pricing compare, with a calculator
- Free options for small projects
:::

{{< include ../_series-nav.md >}}

## Who manages what

Moving from left to right, the provider takes over more of the work. You gain convenience and lose some control. Pick a level to see the split.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {ms, msStyle} from "/assets/js/ms-plot.js"
levels = ["Virtual machine", "Kubernetes", "Serverless container", "Managed ML platform"]
viewof lvl = Inputs.radio(levels, {value: "Serverless container", label: "Run on"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const stack = ["Model and code", "Endpoint and scaling rules", "Container runtime", "Autoscaling", "Operating system and patches", "Servers and network"];
  const yours = {"Virtual machine": 6, "Kubernetes": 4, "Serverless container": 1, "Managed ML platform": 1};
  const n = yours[lvl], W = 760, h = 38;
  const notes = {
    "Virtual machine": "Full control, full responsibility. Good for steady traffic and custom setups.",
    "Kubernetes": "The cluster runs many services. Powerful, but needs platform skills.",
    "Serverless container": "Push a container, get a URL. Scales to zero when idle.",
    "Managed ML platform": "Training, registry, endpoints and monitoring in one product."
  };
  return htl.html`<div>${htl.svg`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${stack.length * (h + 6) + 30}" style="width:100%;max-width:${W}px;font-family:Inter,system-ui,sans-serif">
    ${stack.map((s, i) => htl.svg`<g>
      <rect x="10" y="${i * (h + 6)}" width="${W - 20}" height="${h}" rx="8" fill="${i < n ? ms.indigo : ms.teal}" fill-opacity="${i < n ? 0.85 : 0.25}"/>
      <text x="30" y="${i * (h + 6) + h / 2 + 5}" font-size="13.5" font-weight="600" fill="${i < n ? "white" : "currentColor"}">${s}</text>
      <text x="${W - 30}" y="${i * (h + 6) + h / 2 + 5}" text-anchor="end" font-size="12.5" fill="${i < n ? "white" : "currentColor"}">${i < n ? "You" : "Cloud provider"}</text></g>`)}
  </svg>`}<div class="ms-readout"><span>${lvl}</span><b style="font-size:1rem">${notes[lvl]}</b></div></div>`;
}
```

## The same menu on three clouds

| What you need | AWS | Google Cloud | Azure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Virtual machines | EC2 | Compute Engine | Virtual Machines |
| Serverless containers | App Runner, Lambda (container images) | Cloud Run | Container Apps |
| Managed Kubernetes | EKS | GKE | AKS |
| Managed ML platform | SageMaker AI | Vertex AI | Azure Machine Learning |
| Object storage for models | S3 | Cloud Storage | Blob Storage |
| Container registry | ECR | Artifact Registry | Container Registry |

: Equivalent services across clouds {#tbl-clouds}

Amazon's ML platform is now called **Amazon SageMaker AI** ([AWS](https://aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/ai/)). The concepts carry across clouds, so learning one makes the others easy.

## Traffic shape decides the bill

Most models are not busy all day. Below is a simulated week of PayGuard traffic for a small online shop: busy evenings, quiet nights, a weekend peak.

```{python}
#| label: fig-traffic
#| fig-cap: "Simulated requests per minute over one week. An always-on server is sized for the peak and sits mostly idle."
#| code-fold: true
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, plotly.graph_objects as go
from ms_charts import COLORS, PLOTLY_CONFIG
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
t = pd.date_range("2026-09-07", periods=7 * 24 * 60, freq="min")
h = t.hour + t.minute / 60
daily = 4 + 30 * np.exp(-((h - 20) ** 2) / 8) + 12 * np.exp(-((h - 12.5) ** 2) / 3)
weekend = np.where(t.dayofweek >= 5, 1.5, 1.0)
rpm = rng.poisson(daily * weekend)
peak = np.percentile(rpm, 99.5)
hourly = pd.Series(rpm, index=t).resample("15min").mean()
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_scatter(x=hourly.index, y=hourly.values, fill="tozeroy", name="Requests per minute",
                line=dict(color=COLORS["indigo"], width=1.5), fillcolor="rgba(99,102,241,0.25)")
fig.add_hline(y=peak, line_dash="dash", line_color=COLORS["rose"], annotation_text="Always-on server sized for peak", annotation_position="top left")
fig.update_layout(height=360, yaxis_title="Requests per minute", showlegend=False)
fig.show(config=PLOTLY_CONFIG)
util = rpm.mean() / peak
```

On average the traffic uses only **`{python} f"{util:.0%}"`** of the peak capacity. With an always-on server you pay for 100% of it, all week. With **serverless**, you pay per request and per second of compute, and it can **scale to zero** at night.

## Cost calculator

The prices below are **example values**, not quotes. Replace them with current numbers from your provider's pricing page. The chart shows the monthly cost of each option as traffic grows.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof reqDay = Inputs.range([1000, 5e6], {value: 50000, step: 1000, label: "Requests per day", transform: Math.log})
viewof msReq = Inputs.range([5, 500], {value: 40, step: 5, label: "Compute time per request (ms)"})
viewof vmHour = Inputs.number({value: 0.05, step: 0.01, label: "Always-on server, $ per hour (example)"})
viewof vmCount = Inputs.range([1, 4], {value: 2, step: 1, label: "Servers kept on (for redundancy)"})
viewof perMillion = Inputs.number({value: 0.40, step: 0.05, label: "Serverless, $ per million requests (example)"})
viewof perVcpuS = Inputs.number({value: 0.000024, step: 0.000001, label: "Serverless, $ per vCPU-second (example)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
costVM = r => vmHour * 24 * 30 * vmCount
costSL = r => (r * 30 / 1e6) * perMillion + r * 30 * (msReq / 1000) * perVcpuS
curve = d3.range(3, 6.75, 0.05).map(e => 10 ** e).flatMap(r => [{r, cost: costVM(r), option: "Always-on servers"}, {r, cost: costSL(r), option: "Serverless"}])
breakEven = curve.filter(d => d.option === "Serverless").find(d => d.cost > costVM(d.r))
Plot.plot({
  ...msStyle, height: 360, width: 760, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {type: "log", label: "Requests per day →"}, y: {label: "↑ $ per month", grid: true},
  color: {domain: ["Always-on servers", "Serverless"], range: [ms.rose, ms.teal], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(curve, {x: "r", y: "cost", stroke: "option", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleX([reqDay], {stroke: ms.indigo, strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    breakEven ? Plot.ruleX([breakEven.r], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.4}) : null,
    breakEven ? Plot.text([breakEven], {x: "r", y: d => costVM(d.r), text: d => `break-even ≈ ${d3.format(".2s")(d.r)}/day`, dy: -12, fill: "currentColor", fontSize: 12}) : null
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="ms-readout"><span>At ${d3.format(",")(reqDay)} requests a day</span><b>$${costSL(reqDay).toFixed(2)} serverless vs $${costVM(reqDay).toFixed(2)} always-on</b><span>${costSL(reqDay) < costVM(reqDay) ? "Serverless is cheaper at this volume." : "Steady high volume favours always-on servers."}</span></div>`
```

The pattern is general: **pay-per-use wins at low or spiky traffic; reserved capacity wins at steady high traffic.** Many teams start serverless and move to reserved servers or Kubernetes when volume becomes large and steady.

## Choosing a platform

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart TD
  A[New model to deploy] --> B{Need a GPU?}
  B -- yes --> C{Large team and<br/>many models?}
  C -- yes --> D[Managed ML platform<br/>or Kubernetes with GPUs]
  C -- no --> E[Managed ML endpoint<br/>or GPU VM]
  B -- no --> F{Traffic spiky<br/>or low?}
  F -- yes --> G[Serverless container<br/>Cloud Run, Container Apps, App Runner]
  F -- no --> H{Already run<br/>Kubernetes?}
  H -- yes --> I[Deploy to EKS, GKE or AKS]
  H -- no --> J[Small VM group<br/>behind a load balancer]
```

## Deploying PayGuard to a serverless container

Google Cloud Run is a good example of the serverless path: build the image, push it, deploy it.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
# build and push to Artifact Registry
gcloud builds submit --tag \
  us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/ml/payguard:1.4.0

# deploy: scale to zero when idle, at most 10 instances
gcloud run deploy payguard \
  --image us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/ml/payguard:1.4.0 \
  --region us-central1 --port 8000 \
  --min-instances 0 --max-instances 10 \
  --cpu 1 --memory 1Gi
```

The same container works on AWS App Runner or Azure Container Apps with their own commands. That portability is the reward for using Docker.

## Free and low-cost options

For learning projects and small sites, you can often pay nothing:

- **Google Cloud Run** has a monthly free tier; with request-based billing it includes **2 million requests, 180,000 vCPU-seconds and 360,000 GiB-seconds** ([Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/run/pricing)).
- **Hugging Face Spaces** offers a free **CPU Basic** tier with 2 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory, good for Gradio or Streamlit demos ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-overview)).
- AWS and Azure also offer free tiers and starter credits; check their current terms.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Set a budget alert on day one
Every cloud lets you create a budget with email alerts. A forgotten GPU instance can cost more in a weekend than a year of serverless traffic.
:::

## Summary

- Four levels: **VM, Kubernetes, serverless container, managed ML platform**. Higher levels mean less work and less control.
- AWS, Google Cloud and Azure offer **equivalent services** under different names.
- **Spiky or low traffic favours serverless**; steady heavy traffic favours reserved servers.
- Keep the model in a container so you can move between clouds.
- Next: handle traffic spikes in [Scale](/deployment/scale/scaling-ml-inference.qmd).
